overview: The PEACE in Sudan Act responds to the ongoing war in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group. It lets the President freeze U.S. assets and block transactions of foreign people or companies that arm either side, commit atrocities, block humanitarian aid, use child soldiers, smuggle gold or gum arabic, or undermine peace talks. It extends the term of the U.S. Special Envoy for Sudan, requires reports on foreign governments' roles in the war and on atrocities, and asks whether any armed group should be labeled a terrorist. It also limits direct U.S. aid and debt relief to Sudan's government and directs U.S. officials at the World Bank and similar lenders to oppose early reconstruction loans, with exceptions for lifesaving humanitarian projects and presidential waivers. Most requirements end once a verified peace is reached, and the whole law expires after 5 years. As of July 27, 2026, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had approved it and it was waiting for a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say the bill gives the United States stronger tools to pressure armed groups and their foreign backers, protect civilians and push toward a peace deal in one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
against: Critics say sanctions and limits on aid and lending could make it harder to rebuild Sudan and may hurt ordinary Sudanese people, even with the humanitarian exceptions and waivers.
